thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: Banking discipline: broken, evidenced by widespread misconduct and cultural failure [D01], [D07].
Low-cost operations: broken, evidenced by high expense/revenue ratio and ongoing remediation costs [D03].
Growth: broken, due to persistent Federal Reserve asset-growth restrictions [D03], [D07].
final.price_vs_value_now: Market cap $88.6bn [D04]; trading at ~0.67x tangible book [D04], reflecting lasting compliance costs and restricted growth [D04].
final.after_tax_hurdle: The business's fundamental economic advantage has deteriorated [D01], meaning current market value, despite the discount to book, does not justify the capital risk or opportunity cost [D06].

drivers.driver: The institutional culture and sales-practices failures have fundamentally damaged the competitive advantage that originally justified the investment [D01], [D05].
Persistent regulatory asset caps and high remediation expenses have structurally impaired the bank's earning power [D03], [D05].
The future of the business has become unknowable, as trust repair and culture reform are expensive and uncertain [D01], [D05].
Better capital allocation opportunities exist within the broader financial sector and Berkshire's portfolio [D06], [D08].

final.memo:
When we invest in a bank, we look for low-cost operations and sound banking discipline. The events that have come to light at Wells Fargo since 2016 demonstrate a profound institutional failure that is not easily fixed [D01], [D07]. A bank's deposit franchise can survive for a time, but the culture and compliance costs that follow such widespread misconduct permanently reduce what owners can earn [D01]. 

We no longer have confidence that the bank's competitive advantage is durable or that its future path is predictable [D01], [D05]. The asset growth restriction imposed by the Federal Reserve remains binding, limiting the bank's ability to operate effectively, while remediation and litigation continue to weigh on earnings [D03], [D07]. We do not wait for a full recovery when the underlying economic thesis has been broken by systemic issues [D01], [D05]. 

It is our practice to exit when the world has changed and the business's fundamental advantage is lost [S1]. While the stock may appear cheap relative to tangible book value, that discount reflects the reality of constrained growth and lasting compliance obligations [D04], [D06]. We are not in the business of holding companies through prolonged periods of structural repair when our capital can be better deployed elsewhere [D06].
